drills.q: What was the older storage interface shaped for?
options: A device with one arm that reorders requests to reduce head movement
A device with many independent chips
A network attached array
Sequential access from tape
drills.why: Thirty-two outstanding commands is plenty for a device that can only do one thing at a time, and nowhere near enough for one with dozens of chips.

drills.q: Why was a fast drive on that interface idle?
options: The host could not have enough requests outstanding to reach every chip
The wire was too slow
The controller could not keep up
The medium could not sustain the rate
drills.why: The bottleneck was not the medium, the controller or the wire. It was the shape of the conversation, which is why the answer was a new interface rather than a faster one.

drills.q: What is the intended queue arrangement in NVMe?
options: One submission and completion pair per processor core
One deep queue shared by all cores
One queue per NAND chip
One queue per open file
drills.why: The depth is the headline and this is the design: no two cores need ever touch the same memory to talk to the device.

drills.q: Why does a queue per core matter more than the depth?
options: A shared queue needs a lock, and a contended lock's cost grows with the core count
Each core gets its own bandwidth allocation
It allows different priorities per core
It reduces interrupt routing overhead
drills.why: Submitting to a private queue touches only memory that core already owns, which is why the per-command cost stopped rising as machines grew more cores.

drills.q: What decides how many requests must be outstanding to keep a device busy?
options: Throughput times latency
Throughput divided by latency
The number of chips in the device
The queue depth the interface allows
drills.why: A million operations a second at a hundred microseconds each means a hundred in flight. Ask for fewer and the device is idle rather than slow.

drills.q: A benchmark issues one request at a time. What did it measure?
options: Latency, correctly, and reported it as throughput
Throughput, correctly
Nothing meaningful
The interface's per-command overhead
drills.why: Queue depth one tells you what an interactive operation waits for, and high queue depth tells you what a batch job gets. A single number describes neither.

drills.q: What does the doorbell do, and why does it cost?
options: A write to a device register across the bus, which leaves the processor's own memory
Signals an interrupt to the host
Copies the command to the device
Flushes the submission queue to NAND
drills.why: Which is why several commands can be placed in the ring and one doorbell announces all of them, so the per-command cost of reaching the device falls with the batch size.

options: Latency, up to the timer's duration, for a divided interrupt cost
Throughput for latency
Correctness for speed
Memory for processor time
drills.why: A good trade for a batch job and a bad one for a request somebody is waiting on.

options: When the completion rate is high enough that the core would have been busy anyway
Always, since it removes a kernel transition
When latency does not matter
On single-core machines
drills.why: Below that rate it is a core spent on nothing, which is why the kernel supports all three schemes: the right choice depends on a ratio it cannot know.

drills.q: Does an NVMe command contain the data?
options: No; it describes where in host memory the data lives
Yes, for transfers up to 4 KB
Yes, always
Only for writes
drills.why: Which is why asking for four kilobytes and asking for a megabyte cost the same submission, the same doorbell and the same completion.

drills.q: Why are small requests expensive per byte?
options: The per-request cost is fixed and the per-byte cost is small
Small requests are more likely to be misaligned
The device batches them internally
They defeat the read-ahead
drills.why: A workload doing four-kilobyte reads spends most of its budget on bookkeeping, and the same bytes read in megabytes spends almost none.

drills.q: What was wrong with the old block layer?
options: One locked queue per device and a scheduler optimising for a constraint that had gone
It could not address large devices
It lacked support for asynchronous requests
It copied every request through a bounce buffer
drills.why: On a machine with many cores the lock was the limit, and the reordering was work spent on head movement for a mechanism that no longer existed.

drills.q: What is the best scheduler for a device with no seek time?
options: Barely a scheduler
The same one, with a shorter time window
One that sorts by logical address
One that groups requests by erase block
drills.why: The layer it replaced was not wrong. It had stopped earning its cost, which is a shape that recurs whenever a constraint disappears.

drills.q: A device can do a million operations a second and the software costs five microseconds each. What is delivered?
options: Two hundred thousand
A million
Five million
It depends on the queue depth
drills.why: Every one of those five microseconds is software, which is why the interesting storage engineering of the last decade has been about removing host overhead rather than making devices faster.

drills.q: Where has the storage bottleneck ended up?
options: In the operating system, after moving from the medium and then the interface
Still in the medium
In the PCIe bus
In the filesystem's metadata
drills.why: Each move made the previous layer's cleverness redundant, which is why the software above the device has been getting thinner rather than more capable.
